watchForNext.neutral: You might hear them playing with sounds, like 'c-a-t, cat!' or 'what starts with mmm?', and pairing letters with the sounds they make, not just their names. Some children start spotting a familiar short word on a page or a sign.

variants.charlotte_mason: Watch for interest in how words are built, new words made by changing one letter, and for a few words recognised from a favourite rhyme they know by heart.
variants.classical: As letter sounds are learned through songs and chants, listen for sounds blended aloud into short words, and for the first sound of a word named without a pause.
variants.montessori: After the sandpaper letters, watch for the child tracing a letter while saying its sound, playing 'I spy' unprompted, and reaching for the moveable alphabet to build a word.
variants.waldorf_steiner: Letters are usually met through pictures and stories here, around age seven. Before then, watch for delight in alliteration and verse, and for sounds played with in songs and games.
variants.unschooling: Look for sound games woven into the day, rhyming nonsense, 'I spy', guessing what a word starts with, and curiosity about what the letters on a packet or sign say.
variants.eclectic: Watch for letter sounds, not just letter names, coming up in play, and for first attempts at sounding out a short word on a page or a sign.

watchForNext.neutral: Instead of counting everything from one, you might notice them starting from the bigger number and counting on. Watch too for a few small sums, like doubles, being known without needing to count.

variants.charlotte_mason: With real things like buttons, beans or apples, watch for counting on from the larger group instead of from one, and for small story sums solved in the head.
variants.classical: As number facts become memory work, listen for doubles recited and then used, 'four and four is eight', and for counting on from the bigger number in a sum.
variants.montessori: With the short bead stair and number rods, watch for the child counting on from the first quantity, and for interest in writing the sum down once the beads have shown the answer.
variants.waldorf_steiner: Number stories and counting rhymes carry a lot here. Watch for small sums solved inside a story, such as how many acorns the squirrel has left, without recounting every acorn.
variants.unschooling: Look for adding and taking away in play, how many more turns, how many biscuits are left, how many pieces each, worked out more quickly than counting from one.
variants.eclectic: Whether with blocks, counters or snacks, watch for counting on from the bigger group, and for doubles known by heart.

watchForNext.neutral: You might hear counting start from a number other than one, or run backwards like a rocket launch. Watch too for a guess at 'how many' before counting, and for interest in numbers past twenty.

variants.charlotte_mason: On walks and at the table, watch for a guess at how many acorns or stones before counting to check, and for counting that can start anywhere or run backwards.
variants.classical: As counting chants grow longer, listen for counting on from any number, counting back, and the first skip counting by tens.
variants.montessori: After the number rods and spindle boxes, watch for numeral cards matched to quantities beyond ten, and for interest in the teen and ten boards.
variants.waldorf_steiner: Watch for counting carried in rhythm, through stepping, clapping or skipping rope, that can start from any number and run backwards too.
variants.unschooling: Look for numbers taking on a life in play: counting down to a race start, guessing how many strawberries are in the punnet, or reading the numbers in a lift.
variants.eclectic: Watch for counting that can start from any number or run backwards, and for a guess at 'how many' before the count begins.

watchForNext.neutral: Letters may start to settle into a steadier size and sit along an imagined line. Watch too for small gaps appearing between words, and for writing beyond their own name, like a label or a sibling's name.

variants.charlotte_mason: In early copywork of a single letter or word, watch for one carefully formed letter rather than many careless ones, and for that care carried into writing their name on drawings.
variants.classical: As letter formation is practised, watch for letters started in the right place and made the same way each time, and for copied words with a space between them.
variants.montessori: After the sandpaper letters and metal insets, watch for steadier, more controlled lines, and for labels, names and short words written for the child's own purposes.
variants.waldorf_steiner: Form drawing comes before letters here. Watch for straight and curved lines drawn with growing confidence, and for those forms beginning to appear in their first capital letters.
variants.unschooling: Look for writing with a purpose of their own, their name on a drawing, a 'keep out' sign, a card for Nan, with letters becoming easier to read.
variants.eclectic: Watch for letters becoming more even in size and starting to sit on a line, whether on a practice page or a birthday card.

watchForNext.neutral: A label may grow into a sentence, and one sentence into two or three that follow on from each other. You might also notice describing words creeping in, like 'the huge, scary dog'.

variants.charlotte_mason: Oral narration comes before written composition here. Watch for spoken narrations growing longer and better ordered, and for the child asking you to write one down so they can illustrate it.
variants.classical: Watch for a dictated sentence becoming a short paragraph, and for the child copying out a sentence they composed aloud, capital letter and full stop in place.
variants.montessori: With the moveable alphabet, watch for words becoming phrases and then little stories, composed long before the hand can write them all.
variants.waldorf_steiner: Watch for a short sentence of the child's own appearing under a main lesson book picture, often growing from a verse or story told that week.
variants.unschooling: Look for writing that carries a message, a note left on the fridge, a list for the holidays, a caption under a drawing, and for one sentence becoming two.
variants.eclectic: Whether dictated, typed or handwritten, watch for single labels growing into connected sentences, and for describing words chosen on purpose.

watchForNext.neutral: You might notice them stopping to look closely without being asked, and pointing out more than one thing at once: the colour, the legs, the way it moves. Watch too for 'it's different from last time' about a plant or puddle they've seen before.

variants.charlotte_mason: On regular nature walks, watch for the child stopping to look closely without a reminder, and for two or three details of what they found described when you get home.
variants.classical: Watch for the child naming what they see and listing its parts, petals, stem and leaves, and for questions about what something is called.
variants.montessori: Watch for long, quiet looking at a leaf or insect, chosen by the child, and for a magnifier picked up without being suggested.
variants.waldorf_steiner: On daily walks through the seasons, watch for the child noticing the same tree changing and greeting it like an old friend, with wonder lingering a little longer each time.
variants.unschooling: Look for the child calling you over to see something, a beetle, a cloud, a strange seed, and staying with it long enough to notice more than one thing about it.
variants.eclectic: On walks or in the backyard, watch for close looking without a reminder, and for 'it's changed!' about something they've seen before.

watchForNext.neutral: Questions may move from 'is it alive?' to 'what does it turn into?', with an interest in eggs, seeds and caterpillars. You might also see them sorting creatures or plants by what they have in common, such as legs, wings or shells.

variants.charlotte_mason: In nature study, watch for the child following one creature or plant over weeks, a silkworm, a bean or a tadpole, and narrating how it has changed.
variants.classical: As the names of living things are learned, watch for grouping by features, birds have feathers and insects have six legs, and for the stages of a life cycle recited in order.
variants.montessori: After living and non-living sorting and the botany puzzles, watch for interest in life cycles, and for animals classified by body covering or how they move.
variants.waldorf_steiner: Watch for wonder at growth and change through the seasons: seeds planted and watched in the garden, and stories of how creatures live turning into the child's own questions.
variants.unschooling: Look for a pet, garden patch or backyard visitor sparking questions about what it eats, where it sleeps and how it grows, and for the learner hunting down the answers.
variants.eclectic: Whether from a science lesson or the garden, watch for interest in how things grow and change, and for creatures sorted by what they have in common.

watchForNext.neutral: Spelling may start to follow patterns, such as cat, hat and mat, and common words like 'the' and 'said' come out right more often. You might also see them pause, frown at a word, and try it another way.

variants.charlotte_mason: Watch for the child looking hard at a word to picture it, then spelling it correctly from memory, a habit that grows out of careful copywork.
variants.classical: As spelling rules and lists are learned, watch for those patterns in the child's own writing, and for word families recited and stretched: cat, hat, mat... flat!
variants.montessori: With the moveable alphabet and phonogram cards, watch for words built with the letter pairs they've learned, and for a word checked against a card on their own.
variants.waldorf_steiner: Watch for words copied with care from the board into the main lesson book appearing correctly spelled in the child's own sentences.
variants.unschooling: Look for spelling questions that come from things they want to write, 'how do you spell dinosaur?', and for words seen often in games and signs spelled right.
variants.eclectic: Whatever spelling approach you use, watch for patterns from word lists turning up in their own writing, and for a pause when a word 'doesn't look right'.

watchForNext.neutral: Questions about the past may grow bigger, like 'did they have cars when Nan was little?'. You might also notice events put in order beyond their own life, and wondering about how people lived long ago.

variants.charlotte_mason: As history is read from living books, watch for a story from long ago narrated with its people vividly remembered, and for questions about where it fits beside other stories they know.
variants.classical: As the first history stories and timeline cards are introduced, watch for people and events remembered by name, and for curiosity about what came before and after.
variants.montessori: After making a timeline of their own life, watch for interest in longer timelines, of the family, the town and the earth, and for questions about how people met their needs long ago.
variants.waldorf_steiner: History lives first in story here, in fairy tales, fables and legends. Watch for the child asking whether a story 'really happened', often the first sign of a sense of the past.
variants.unschooling: Look for history arriving through family stories, old photos and outings: questions about what Grandad did as a kid, or how people managed before electricity.
variants.eclectic: Whether it's a history read-aloud or an afternoon with old photo albums, listen for 'how did people live back then?', and watch for events put in order beyond their own lifetime.

watchForNext.neutral: Builds may start to be made for someone, a ramp for a little sibling or a box that a toy actually fits in, with that person in mind. You might also hear them weighing up choices, like 'taller looks better but it keeps falling'.

variants.charlotte_mason: In handicrafts and building projects, watch for something useful made well for someone else, a gift or a fix around the house, and for the child explaining what they changed and why.
variants.classical: Watch for a design explained in order, the problem, the plan, what was tested and what changed, and for labelled drawings that record each version.
variants.montessori: Watch for long, self-directed projects where the child sets their own standard, revising the work until it does the job they chose for it.
variants.waldorf_steiner: In woodwork, sewing and making, watch for practical things made with care, a bag that holds what it should or a bridge that carries weight, adjusted until it works.
variants.unschooling: Look for projects with a real audience or use, a cubby, a marble run for friends, a stall for a market day, and for versions improved after watching others use them.
variants.eclectic: Whether from a design kit or the recycling bin, watch for builds made with someone else in mind, and for choices explained: what they gave up and why.
